You explained the idea yesterday. Today a colleague presents it as theirs. If you can respond calmly, make your contribution specific: “I’m glad we’re taking this forward. When I proposed the pilot yesterday, the problem I wanted to solve was the handover delay. I can walk us through the first step.”

If the meeting has moved on, follow up privately: “In today’s meeting, you presented the pilot without mentioning my contribution. I developed the proposal we discussed yesterday. Can you clarify that in the follow-up?”

Use details you can support. If this keeps happening, keep the relevant drafts and messages, and discuss the pattern with a manager you trust. You do not have to improvise a confrontation with someone who can retaliate against you.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Remedy the situation It’s not enough to address the credit stealing. You also need to make the situation right, i.e. get the credit you deserve. If the other person recognizes their mistake, you might request that they send an email acknowledging your contributions, or you can both talk to your manager to set the record straight. 6. Be proactive about preventing it from happening again How can you make sure you get credit in the future? If you feel like you’re being systematically undermined, Dillon suggests talking to your boss or another manager. And Uzzi’s research shows that in collaborative projects, it’s important to agree upfront on allocation, and even write down a plan for how people will get credit. Never assume the roles are clear to everyone! 7. Model good credit sharing You can set the right tone by giving credit where it’s due. For example, Uzzi likes to add a slide at the end of his presentations with the name of every contributor. He tries to give his collaborators the deck beforehand and ask, “Does it give appropriate credit?” I love this approach! Check out the full article for more concrete examples and detail. One important note about the article: I wrote it nine years ago and regret not including some of the important nuances around gender and credit stealing. This is a topic that my Women at Work colleagues explored in an early episode of the podcast: The Art of Claiming Credit . I highly recommend listening to it to learn more about the ways that gender bias influences who gets credit and why. Now, I’m curious: if you’ve been in this situation, what helped you to get out of it? Did you decide to let it go, or did you say something?
